questions.stem: All hormones react to a negative feedback except:
questions.why: Oxytocin release during labour is a classic positive-feedback reflex. Cervical stretch increases oxytocin release, contractions intensify and further stretch occurs until delivery interrupts the cycle. Negative feedback predominates in many endocrine axes.

notes.A: Progesterone typically slows hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility and contributes to negative feedback on gonadotropin release.
notes.B: Oestradiol usually provides negative feedback. Sustained high oestradiol before ovulation can temporarily switch the response to positive feedback and trigger the LH surge.
notes.C: Prolactin can increase hypothalamic dopamine release, which feeds back to inhibit prolactin secretion.
notes.E: The labour reflex provides a clear example of oxytocin amplifying the stimulus that caused its release.

questions.stem: Lipid hormones derived from cholesterol are:
questions.why: Steroid hormones are synthesised from cholesterol. The adrenal cortex and gonads convert cholesterol to pregnenolone and then to different steroid hormones, depending on the enzymes expressed.

notes.A: Protein hormones are chains of amino acids synthesised by ribosomes, not derivatives of cholesterol.
notes.B: Amino acid-derived hormones include catecholamines and thyroid hormones, which are derived from tyrosine.
notes.C: Polypeptide hormones are synthesised from amino acids as precursors that can be processed before secretion.
notes.E: Eicosanoids are derived from polyunsaturated fatty acids such as arachidonic acid, rather than from cholesterol.

questions.stem: This type of hormone must bind to a receptor protein on the plasma membrane of the cell:
questions.why: Water-soluble peptide hormones generally cannot cross the lipid bilayer directly. They bind to receptors on the cell surface, which convey the signal through intracellular pathways.

notes.B: Many lipid-soluble hormones can reach intracellular receptors. Some lipid-derived signals use surface receptors, so this broad class does not require them exclusively.
notes.C: Steroid hormones commonly cross into target cells and act on intracellular receptors that regulate gene expression.
notes.D: Polypeptides normally signal through surface receptors, while many lipid-soluble hormones use intracellular receptors.
notes.E: Steroids are lipid-soluble and often bind cytoplasmic or nuclear receptors to alter transcription.

questions.stem: Endocrine glands release hormones in response to:
questions.why: Endocrine secretion can respond to another hormone, to a change in the blood, or to a neural signal. Examples include TSH acting on the thyroid, glucose stimulating insulin and sympathetic nerves activating the adrenal medulla.

notes.A: A tropic hormone can regulate another gland. For example, TSH stimulates thyroid hormone production and release.
notes.B: Changes in circulating substances can directly control secretion. Rising blood glucose promotes insulin release.
notes.C: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons can stimulate adrenal chromaffin cells to release catecholamines.
notes.E: Each of the listed mechanisms provides a recognised route for regulating endocrine secretion.

questions.stem: The anterior pituitary secretes:
questions.why: Corticotrophs in the anterior pituitary process pro-opiomelanocortin into ACTH and other peptides. Beta-endorphin derives from the same precursor, and pituitary release can increase during stress.

notes.A: Oxytocin is made by hypothalamic neurons and released from their endings in the posterior pituitary.
notes.C: Vasopressin is made in the hypothalamus, then carried to the posterior pituitary for release.
notes.D: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone comes from the hypothalamus. It travels in portal blood to stimulate anterior pituitary TSH secretion.
notes.E: Catecholamines are released mainly from sympathetic neurons and the adrenal medulla, rather than being anterior pituitary hormones.

questions.stem: Gland which shrinks in size during adulthood, and has hormones that function in the maturation of T-lymphocytes:
questions.why: The thymus is the primary site of T-cell differentiation and selection, supported by thymic epithelial cells and their signalling molecules. It undergoes involution after puberty, although some functional tissue remains.

notes.A: Lymph nodes support immune responses to antigens in lymph. Mature T cells respond there after their principal developmental selection in the thymus.
notes.C: The spleen filters blood and supports responses to blood-borne antigens. It is not the primary site of T-cell development.
notes.D: Gut-associated lymphoid tissue supports mucosal immunity and tolerance. Its lymphocytes are not selected there in the same way as developing thymocytes.
notes.E: Tonsils sample inhaled and ingested antigens. They are secondary lymphoid structures, unlike the thymus.

questions.stem: Adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) secretion increases:

options.label: A
options.text: when the median eminence of the hypothalamus is stimulated

options.label: C
options.text: in bursts during the night as the normal hour of wakening approaches

questions.why: Hypothalamic CRH and vasopressin stimulate ACTH secretion. Reduced cortisol removes negative feedback, ACTH pulses increase toward the usual waking period, and major stress can activate this axis.

notes.A: Stimulating relevant hypothalamic terminals in the median eminence can release CRH into portal blood and increase ACTH.
notes.B: A fall in cortisol reduces inhibition of hypothalamic and pituitary signalling, allowing ACTH to rise.
notes.C: Pulses of ACTH tend to increase late in the sleep period before the usual time of awakening.
notes.D: Severe trauma activates the stress response and can increase hypothalamic drive to anterior pituitary corticotrophs.

questions.stem: Melatonin:

options.label: A
options.text: is produced mainly in the pineal gland

options.label: B
options.text: is synthesized in the body from serotonin

options.label: C
options.text: blood levels are highest during the night

options.label: D
options.text: influences the secretion rates of pituitary hormones

questions.why: The pineal gland makes melatonin from serotonin and releases most of it at night. Melatonin signals biological night and can affect endocrine timing, including regulation of pituitary hormone secretion in some settings.

notes.A: The pineal gland is the main source of the rhythmic melatonin signal found in circulating blood.
notes.B: Serotonin is converted to N-acetylserotonin and then to melatonin in pineal cells.
notes.C: Pineal melatonin secretion normally rises in darkness and decreases with light exposure at night.
notes.D: Melatonin can influence hypothalamic–pituitary signalling, with effects depending on the species, hormone and timing.

questions.stem: The growth hormone:

options.label: A
options.text: promotes positive nitrogen and phosphorus balance

options.label: D
options.text: stimulates the liver to secrete somatomedins which regulate bone and cartilage growth

questions.why: Growth hormone promotes protein synthesis and retention of nitrogen and phosphate. Hypothalamic signals regulate its pulses, a prominent pulse occurs during sleep, and insulin-like growth factor 1 mediates many of its effects on bone and cartilage.

notes.A: Growth hormone increases protein anabolism and can promote renal phosphate retention during growth.
notes.B: Hypothalamic GHRH stimulates release, while hypothalamic somatostatin restrains it.
notes.C: A major growth hormone pulse is normally associated with deep non-REM sleep, especially early in the night.
notes.D: The liver secretes circulating IGF-1 in response to growth hormone. Locally produced IGF-1 also contributes to skeletal growth.

questions.stem: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin):

options.label: A
options.text: is released from nerve endings in the posterior pituitary gland

options.label: B
options.text: tends to raise the osmolality of plasma

options.label: C
options.text: increases the permeability of the cells to water in the loop of Henle

options.label: D
options.text: secretion is little affected by changes in plasma osmolality

questions.why: Vasopressin is made in hypothalamic neurons and transported down their axons to nerve endings in the posterior pituitary. From there it enters the blood and promotes water reabsorption in collecting ducts.

notes.B: Increased water reabsorption generally lowers plasma osmolality toward its set point rather than raising it.
notes.C: The principal adjustable water permeability is in the late distal nephron and collecting ducts, through aquaporin-2.
notes.D: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors are sensitive to changes in plasma tonicity, which strongly influences vasopressin release.
notes.E: Vasopressin increases renal water reabsorption and decreases the excretion of free water.

questions.stem: Releasing hormones produced in the hypothalamus:

options.label: A
options.text: are secreted by cells in the median eminence

options.label: B
options.text: pass down blood vessel to reach the pituitary gland

options.label: C
options.text: may control the output of more than one pituitary hormone

questions.why: Hypothalamic releasing hormones enter the hypophyseal portal system to control anterior pituitary secretion.

notes.A: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.B: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.C: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.D: True, but so are the other statements.

questions.stem: The pituitary gland:

options.label: A
options.text: regulates activity in all other endocrine glands

options.label: B
options.text: output of oxytocin is regulated by hypothalamic releasing factors

options.label: C
options.text: responds to nervous and hormonal influences from the brain

options.label: D
options.text: secretes antidiuretic hormone when blood osmolality falls

questions.why: The pituitary responds to both nervous and hormonal (hypothalamic) inputs. It does not regulate ALL other glands (e.g., pancreas is independent).

notes.A: Not all glands, e.g. the endocrine pancreas and parathyroids are independent.
notes.B: Oxytocin is released by nerve impulses, not by releasing factors.
notes.D: ADH is secreted when osmolality RISES.
notes.E: The pituitary does produce MSH (from POMC).

questions.stem: Growth hormone secretion:

options.label: A
options.text: increases when the blood glucose level falls

questions.why: Hypoglycaemia can stimulate growth hormone secretion. Human growth hormone can have lactogenic activity at the prolactin receptor, and persistent excess can enlarge viscera. It also increases hepatic production of IGF-1.

notes.A: A fall in circulating glucose can activate growth hormone release as part of the counter-regulatory response.
notes.B: Human growth hormone can activate the prolactin receptor, although prolactin is the main physiological driver of milk synthesis.
notes.C: Sustained excess growth hormone and IGF-1 can produce enlargement of internal organs, as in acromegaly.
notes.D: Growth hormone stimulates the liver to produce IGF-1, formerly called somatomedin C.

questions.stem: Prolactin:

options.label: A
options.text: has a similar chemical structure and physiological action to luteinizing hormone

options.label: B
options.text: is responsible for breast growth in puberty

options.label: D
options.text: secretion is inhibited by suckling of the breast

options.label: E
options.text: causes ejection of milk by the breast during suckling

questions.why: Hypothalamic dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin secretion through D2 receptors on anterior pituitary lactotrophs. Suckling decreases the inhibitory input, allowing prolactin release to increase.

notes.A: Prolactin is structurally related to growth hormone. LH is a glycoprotein that acts chiefly on the gonads.
notes.B: Oestrogens are major drivers of ductal growth at puberty. Prolactin supports mammary differentiation and milk synthesis, especially around pregnancy and lactation.
notes.D: Suckling increases prolactin by reducing dopaminergic inhibition of lactotrophs.
notes.E: Oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells for milk ejection. Prolactin supports milk production.

questions.stem: When a patient with diabetes insipidus is treated successfully with antidiuretic hormone the:

options.label: A
options.text: urinary flow rate should fall by about 50 per cent

options.label: B
options.text: urinary output should be reduced to around 1 ml/minute

options.label: C
options.text: urinary osmolality should rise to between 100 and 200 mOsm/litre

options.label: E
options.text: salt intake should be carefully regulated

questions.why: In central diabetes insipidus, effective vasopressin replacement increases collecting-duct water reabsorption and reduces dilute polyuria. A urine flow around one millilitre per minute is a representative normal value, not an exact treatment target.

notes.A: The percentage fall depends on starting urine flow, water intake and response. There is no fixed 50 percent reduction.
notes.C: Effective replacement increases the ability to concentrate urine. A urine osmolality of 100–200 still describes dilute urine.
notes.D: Retention of water tends to lower a previously raised plasma osmolality toward normal.
notes.E: The direct response to vasopressin is increased renal water reabsorption. This option does not describe that physiological effect.

questions.stem: A pituitary tumour secreting excess growth hormone (GH) in an adult may lead to:

options.label: C
options.text: reduced levels of somatomedins in blood

questions.why: In adults, excess growth hormone causes acromegaly and can antagonise insulin action in muscle and adipose tissue. The resulting insulin resistance can increase blood glucose despite compensatory insulin secretion.

notes.A: Myxoedema is associated with severe hypothyroidism, not a characteristic direct effect of growth hormone excess.
notes.B: Gigantism occurs if excess growth hormone acts before epiphyseal closure. In adults, the growth plates are closed.
notes.C: Growth hormone usually increases hepatic IGF-1, one of the circulating somatomedins.
notes.D: Severe untreated congenital hypothyroidism causes a different disorder from adult growth hormone excess.

questions.stem: Surgical removal of the pituitary gland is likely to lead to a decrease in:
questions.why: Pituitary removal can cause gonadotropin deficiency and reduce gonadal steroid production. Menstrual cycles can stop, sexual desire and axillary hair can decrease, and loss of hormonal support can reduce mammary tissue.

notes.A: Lower LH and FSH can impair ovarian cyclic activity and decrease the frequency of menstruation.
notes.B: Reduced adrenal and gonadal androgen support can cause loss of axillary hair, particularly in women.
notes.C: Gonadal steroid deficiency can reduce libido, although sexual desire has other determinants as well.
notes.D: Reduced ovarian steroid support can lead to mammary gland involution and a decrease in breast tissue.

questions.stem: Secretion of the growth hormone:
questions.why: The largest sleep-related growth hormone pulse is typically associated with slow-wave non-REM sleep, often during the first deep sleep period. Release is pulsatile and also occurs during wakefulness.

notes.A: The prominent nocturnal pulse is generally linked to deep non-REM sleep rather than REM sleep.
notes.B: Oral glucose often suppresses growth hormone in healthy people. Failure of suppression can occur in acromegaly.
notes.C: Obesity is commonly associated with reduced spontaneous and stimulated growth hormone secretion.
notes.E: Slow-wave non-REM sleep has a well-established association with an increase in growth hormone secretion.

questions.stem: The pineal body (gland):
questions.why: The pineal gland secretes melatonin, particularly during darkness. It lies in the epithalamic region near the roof of the third ventricle and helps signal the timing of biological night.

notes.A: The pineal gland is in the epithalamus. Hypothalamic circadian pathways help regulate its timing.
notes.B: Epinephrine is produced mainly by chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla, rather than by the pineal gland.
notes.D: Hypothalamic and brainstem circuits integrate many appetite signals. The pineal gland is chiefly associated with circadian melatonin.
notes.E: Melanin is a pigment, whereas melatonin is a circulating signalling molecule derived from serotonin.

questions.stem: Excessive growth hormone secretion in adults causes:

options.label: C
options.text: increased entry of glucose in muscles

questions.why: In an adult with closed growth plates, persistent growth hormone excess causes acromegaly. High IGF-1 contributes to enlargement of the hands, feet, jaw, soft tissues and internal organs.

notes.B: Gigantism occurs if excess growth hormone is present before epiphyseal plates close, when long bones can still lengthen.
notes.C: Sustained growth hormone excess often increases insulin resistance and can impair glucose uptake rather than improving it.
notes.D: Hypothyroidism reflects inadequate thyroid hormone action and is not the characteristic consequence of growth hormone excess.
notes.E: Severe untreated congenital hypothyroidism is unrelated to the skeletal and soft tissue effects of adult growth hormone excess.

questions.stem: Thyroid hormones, when secreted in excess, may cause an increase in the:

options.label: C
options.text: energy expenditure required for a given workload

options.label: D
options.text: heart rate when cardiac adrenergic and cholinergic receptors are blocked

questions.why: Thyroid hormone excess increases resting energy expenditure and can increase the oxygen cost of a given workload. It speeds intestinal transit and can raise intrinsic heart rate through direct cardiac effects in addition to autonomic effects.

notes.A: Excess thyroid hormone increases the resting metabolic activity of many tissues, raising basal energy expenditure.
notes.B: Faster gastrointestinal transit can increase the frequency of bowel movements.
notes.C: Increased tissue energy turnover can increase total energy expenditure at a given level of physical work.
notes.D: Thyroid hormone acts directly on cardiac pacemaker and myocardial function, so a higher intrinsic rate can remain after autonomic blockade.

questions.stem: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) secretion is increased:

options.label: A
options.text: after partial removal of the thyroid gland

options.label: B
options.text: in infants born without a thyroid gland

options.label: D
options.text: when the diet is deficient in iodine

questions.why: Reduced thyroid hormone synthesis removes negative feedback and can increase TSH after thyroid tissue loss, thyroid agenesis or iodine deficiency. TSH is also often modestly higher in colder seasons in human populations, although this is variable.

notes.A: If partial thyroid removal lowers hormone output, diminished negative feedback can increase TSH.
notes.B: Thyroid agenesis causes severe primary hypothyroidism, so TSH rises when the pituitary–hypothalamic axis is intact.
notes.C: Many studies report higher average TSH during colder months. The seasonal effect varies between populations and individuals.
notes.D: Inadequate iodine can reduce thyroid hormone synthesis and thereby increase TSH through negative feedback.

questions.stem: Thyroxine:

options.label: A
options.text: increases the resting rate of carbon dioxide production

options.label: B
options.text: is essential for normal development of the brain

options.label: C
options.text: is essential for normal red cell production

questions.why: Thyroxine supports metabolic activity, early brain development and normal erythropoiesis. It acts relatively slowly because much of its action follows conversion to the more active T3, and it circulates with a longer half-life.

notes.A: Increased resting oxidative metabolism increases carbon dioxide production as well as oxygen consumption.
notes.B: Adequate thyroid hormone is crucial for normal brain development during fetal and early postnatal life.
notes.C: Thyroid hormone supports normal erythropoiesis through effects on metabolic demand and erythroid development. Hypothyroidism can cause anaemia.
notes.D: T3 is the more active receptor ligand and generally acts sooner than T4, much of which is converted to T3.

questions.stem: Hyperthyroidism is associated with a:

options.label: C
options.text: clinical picture consistent with excessive beta adrenoceptor stimulation

options.label: E
options.text: rise in the level of thyroxine-binding protein in plasma

questions.why: Tremor, palpitations and tachycardia in hyperthyroidism resemble heightened beta-adrenergic activity. Thyroid hormones also have direct tissue effects, so these signs do not require abnormally high circulating catecholamine levels.

notes.A: Excess thyroid hormone can increase protein breakdown and cause a negative nitrogen balance.
notes.B: Increased bone turnover in thyrotoxicosis can increase urinary calcium, rather than lowering it.
notes.D: Excess thyroid hormone raises resting oxygen use and basal metabolic rate.
notes.E: Thyroxine-binding globulin affects total hormone measurements, but a rise is not a defining feature of hyperthyroidism.

questions.stem: Thyroid hormone stored in the lumen of follicles is in the form of:

options.label: C
options.text: attachment to thyroglobulin in the gland

questions.why: Thyroid follicles store iodinated thyroglobulin in their colloid. T3 and T4 remain part of this protein until thyroglobulin is taken up by follicular cells and proteolysed to release the hormones.

notes.A: T3 is usually released from thyroglobulin after endocytosis and proteolysis. Free T3 is not the main stored form in the follicle.
notes.B: Most stored T4 is incorporated into thyroglobulin rather than stored as free hormone in the colloid.
notes.D: Thyroxine-binding globulin is a circulating transport protein. Thyroglobulin is the colloid storage protein.
notes.E: Thyrotropin is made by the anterior pituitary and stimulates the thyroid. It is not a thyroid hormone stored in follicular colloid.

questions.stem: A high blood calcium level may be due to:
questions.why: Excess parathyroid hormone can raise blood calcium by promoting bone resorption, increasing renal calcium reabsorption and stimulating calcitriol production. Calcitriol in turn increases intestinal calcium absorption.

notes.A: Calcitonin inhibits osteoclast activity and tends to lower rather than raise circulating calcium.
notes.C: Excess glucocorticoids usually reduce intestinal calcium absorption and can promote bone loss without ordinarily causing hypercalcaemia.
notes.D: Glucagon primarily raises blood glucose through effects on liver metabolism. It is not the principal hormone that raises serum calcium.
notes.E: Testosterone influences bone and muscle, but it is not a usual cause of hormone-mediated hypercalcaemia.

questions.stem: Parathormone:

options.label: A
options.text: acts directly on bone to increase bone resorption

options.label: B
options.text: decreases the urinary output of calcium

options.label: D
options.text: promotes absorption of calcium from the intestines

questions.why: PTH acts directly on bone (via osteoblasts signalling to osteoclasts) to release calcium, increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule, blocks phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, and raises gut calcium absorption by activating vitamin D.

notes.A: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.B: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.C: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.D: True, but so are the other statements.

questions.stem: The concentration of ionized calcium in plasma is:

options.label: A
options.text: the main regulator of parathormone secretion

options.label: B
options.text: about 50% of the total plasma calcium concentration

options.label: D
options.text: independent of the plasma albumin changes

questions.why: Ionised calcium is the biologically active fraction and normally accounts for about half of total plasma calcium. It regulates PTH secretion and falls during alkalosis as more calcium binds to albumin. A change in albumin usually affects total calcium more than ionised calcium.

notes.A: Parathyroid calcium-sensing receptors detect free calcium. Low ionised calcium stimulates PTH release.
notes.B: Roughly half of plasma calcium is free. The remainder is bound to proteins or complexed with small anions.
notes.C: Higher pH increases calcium binding to albumin, decreasing ionised calcium even when total calcium changes little.
notes.D: In stable conditions, low albumin can lower measured total calcium without a proportional fall in ionised calcium. Direct measurement is preferable when the distinction matters.

questions.stem: Thyrocalcitonin:

options.label: A
options.text: is produced by the follicular cells of the thyroid gland

options.label: C
options.text: reduces blood calcium in parathyroidectomized animals

options.label: D
options.text: secretion occurs when the blood phosphate level rises

questions.why: Calcitonin can lower blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. It acts directly on osteoclasts, so its calcium-lowering action can occur even when the parathyroid glands have been removed.

notes.A: Calcitonin is secreted by parafollicular C cells. Thyroid follicular cells make T3 and T4.
notes.B: Basal metabolic rate is raised by thyroid hormones such as T3. This is not the principal action of calcitonin.
notes.D: An increase in ionised calcium is the classic physiological stimulus for calcitonin secretion. Phosphate is not the usual primary signal.
notes.E: Calcitonin inhibits osteoclast activity and decreases bone resorption.

questions.stem: Vitamin D:

options.label: A
options.text: increases the intestinal absorption of calcium

options.label: B
options.text: is essential for normal calcification of bones in childhood

questions.why: Vitamin D is hydroxylated in the liver and then the kidney to form calcitriol. Calcitriol increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, supporting bone mineralisation. Deficiency can decrease calcium absorption and lead to secondary hyperparathyroidism.

notes.A: Calcitriol promotes active intestinal calcium uptake by increasing the expression of calcium transport proteins.
notes.B: Adequate vitamin D supports mineralisation of growing bone. Deficiency in children can cause rickets.
notes.C: The liver converts vitamin D to 25-hydroxyvitamin D. The main final activation step occurs in the kidney.
notes.D: Inadequate calcium absorption can increase PTH release as the parathyroid glands respond to the threat to ionised calcium.

questions.stem: Parathormone:

options.label: A
options.text: increases the renal clearance of phosphate

options.label: B
options.text: mobilizes bone calcium independently of its actions on the kidney

options.label: C
options.text: in the blood rises when the calcium level falls

options.label: D
options.text: stimulates the final activation of vitamin D (cholecalciferol) in the kidney

questions.why: Low ionised calcium stimulates PTH secretion. PTH increases renal phosphate clearance, promotes mobilisation of skeletal calcium and stimulates renal production of calcitriol. These effects help defend extracellular calcium.

notes.A: PTH reduces sodium–phosphate cotransporter activity in the proximal tubule, increasing phosphate excretion.
notes.B: Sustained PTH can increase bone resorption through signalling by osteoblast-lineage cells to osteoclasts. This is a separate target-tissue effect from its renal actions.
notes.C: A fall in ionised calcium is sensed by parathyroid calcium-sensing receptors and increases PTH secretion.
notes.D: PTH stimulates proximal tubular 1-alpha-hydroxylase, increasing conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol.

questions.stem: Sudden complete loss of parathyroid function:

options.label: B
options.text: may be fatal if treatment is not given to raise the blood level of ionized calcium

options.label: C
options.text: may be treated in the short-term by slow intravenous injection of calcium ions

options.label: D
options.text: may be treated in the long-term by regular doses of vitamin D

questions.why: Abrupt loss of PTH can cause severe hypocalcaemia and neuromuscular hyperexcitability. Severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia may require monitored intravenous calcium. Long-term treatment commonly includes calcium and an active vitamin D preparation.

notes.A: Low ionised calcium increases neuromuscular excitability and can cause carpopedal spasm or tetany.
notes.B: Severe hypocalcaemia can lead to seizures, laryngospasm or arrhythmias, which can be life-threatening.
notes.C: Intravenous calcium can rapidly restore circulating ionised calcium in severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia and is administered with monitoring.
notes.D: Active vitamin D such as calcitriol helps maintain intestinal calcium absorption when PTH-driven renal activation is impaired.

questions.stem: The risk of tetany is increased by:

options.label: C
options.text: removal of the anterior pituitary gland

questions.why: Tetany is a classic sign of hypocalcemia, which increases the excitability of nerve and muscle tissue.

notes.B: Magnesium lowers excitability.
notes.C: The parathyroids are not pituitary-dependent.
notes.D: Respiratory failure causes acidosis, which RAISES ionised calcium.
notes.E: Renal failure gives acidosis, which protects against tetany.

questions.stem: Thyrocalcitonin:

options.label: A
options.text: is secreted by the thyroid gland

options.label: C
options.text: is secreted by the parathyroid glands

options.label: D
options.text: increases Ca++ absorption by the stomach

questions.why: Calcitonin is secreted by parafollicular C cells of the thyroid gland. Raised circulating ionised calcium stimulates release, and calcitonin can decrease osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.

notes.B: The hypothalamus produces regulatory hormones such as TRH, but is not the source of circulating calcitonin.
notes.C: Parathyroid chief cells secrete PTH, which acts to defend blood calcium when it falls.
notes.D: Calcitonin's characteristic action is inhibition of bone resorption. Regulated dietary calcium absorption occurs mainly in the small intestine.
notes.E: The kidney makes calcitriol and responds to calcium-regulating hormones. Circulating calcitonin comes mainly from the thyroid.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not involved in regulation of plasma Ca++ levels:
questions.why: The lungs are not involved in calcium homeostasis. Kidneys, skin (vitamin D synthesis), intestine, and bones are.

notes.A: Kidneys reabsorb calcium and activate vitamin D.
notes.B: Skin makes vitamin D3.
notes.D: The intestine absorbs calcium.
notes.E: Bone is the calcium store.

questions.stem: Growth of long bones at the epiphyseal plates is mediated mainly by:
questions.why: Growth hormone stimulates production of insulin-like growth factor 1, historically called somatomedin C. Local and circulating IGF-1 contribute to growth plate chondrocyte proliferation and longitudinal bone growth.

notes.A: Calcitonin inhibits osteoclast-mediated resorption. It is not the main mediator of growth hormone at the growth plate.
notes.C: Calcitriol supports calcium and phosphate availability for mineralisation. It does not mediate the principal growth hormone signal to chondrocytes.
notes.D: Thyroid hormone supports normal skeletal development and maturation. The main mediator named in this question is IGF-1.
notes.E: Aldosterone regulates renal sodium and potassium handling. It does not drive chondrocyte proliferation.

questions.stem: Aldosterone secretion is increased by an increase in plasma of:
questions.why: Angiotensin II and extracellular potassium are the main direct stimuli for aldosterone secretion by the zona glomerulosa. Increased renin acts indirectly by raising angiotensin II. ACTH can contribute, usually as a relatively brief or secondary stimulus.

notes.A: Angiotensin II acts on zona glomerulosa cells and increases aldosterone synthesis.
notes.B: A rise in extracellular potassium depolarises glomerulosa cells and increases calcium entry and aldosterone release.
notes.C: Renin increases formation of angiotensin I and then angiotensin II, which is the direct adrenal stimulus.
notes.D: ACTH can transiently increase aldosterone, although it is less important than angiotensin II and potassium for sustained control.

questions.stem: Glucocorticoid injections lead to increases in:
questions.why: Glucocorticoid excess can increase osteoclast-mediated bone resorption early in exposure. With continued exposure, suppression of osteoblast activity and bone formation is especially important in producing osteoporosis.

notes.A: Glucocorticoids can cause involution of lymphoid tissue and decrease immune cell activity rather than enlarge lymph glands.
notes.B: Glucocorticoids suppress fibroblast activity and collagen synthesis, contributing to slower wound repair.
notes.C: Excess glucocorticoids increase muscle protein breakdown and can cause muscle wasting rather than increased anabolism.
notes.E: Inflammatory and immune responses are generally suppressed by glucocorticoid signalling.

questions.stem: Cortisol:

options.label: A
options.text: is bound to an alpha globulin in the plasma

options.label: B
options.text: injections lead to a rise in arterial pressure

options.label: C
options.text: inhibits release of ACTH from the anterior pituitary gland

options.label: D
options.text: is released with a circadian variation so that cortisol blood levels peak in the morning

questions.why: Cortisol circulates mostly bound to corticosteroid-binding globulin and albumin. Its secretion ordinarily peaks near waking, it inhibits ACTH by negative feedback, and elevated glucocorticoid exposure can raise arterial pressure.

notes.A: Corticosteroid-binding globulin, also called transcortin, is an alpha globulin that carries much of circulating cortisol.
notes.B: Glucocorticoids support vascular responsiveness to catecholamines. Sustained or high exposure can also increase blood pressure.
notes.C: Cortisol inhibits both hypothalamic CRH and anterior pituitary ACTH release through negative feedback.
notes.D: Cortisol is secreted in a circadian pattern, with concentrations generally highest near the start of the active period.

questions.stem: Adrenaline secretion from the adrenal glands increases the:

options.label: D
options.text: release of renin in the kidneys

questions.why: Epinephrine mobilises fuel by increasing hepatic glucose output and adipose lipolysis. Beta-2 activation can dilate skeletal muscle vessels at lower concentrations, and beta-1 stimulation can promote renal renin release. Vascular effects vary with receptor activation and dose.

notes.A: Epinephrine increases hepatic glycogenolysis and can raise blood glucose during stress.
notes.B: Adrenergic stimulation of adipose lipolysis releases non-esterified fatty acids into blood.
notes.C: At concentrations that favour beta-2 effects, epinephrine can dilate skeletal muscle vessels. Stronger alpha effects can oppose this.
notes.D: Beta-1 adrenergic activation of juxtaglomerular cells can increase renin release.

questions.stem: Adrenaline differs from noradrenaline in that it:

options.label: A
options.text: increases the heart rate when injected intravenously

options.label: B
options.text: is the main catecholamine secreted by the adrenal medulla

options.label: C
options.text: is a more potent dilator of the bronchi

options.label: D
options.text: dilates blood vessels in skeletal muscle

questions.why: Epinephrine is the predominant catecholamine released by the adrenal medulla. It activates cardiac beta-1 receptors and, through beta-2 receptors, is more effective than noradrenaline at dilating bronchi and skeletal muscle vessels. Net effects after injection depend on dose and reflex responses.

notes.A: Epinephrine can increase heart rate through beta-1 stimulation. Noradrenaline can raise arterial pressure enough to evoke reflex slowing despite its cardiac action.
notes.B: The adrenal medulla converts some noradrenaline to epinephrine, which is usually the larger share of its circulating catecholamine output.
notes.C: Epinephrine provides stronger beta-2-mediated bronchial relaxation than noradrenaline.
notes.D: Beta-2 stimulation can dilate skeletal muscle vessels, especially at lower epinephrine concentrations.

questions.stem: Hormones secreted by the adrenal cortex:

options.label: B
options.text: are mostly bound to plasma proteins

options.label: D
options.text: are excreted mainly in the bile after conjugation

options.label: E
options.text: are essential for the maintenance of pregnancy

questions.why: Most circulating adrenal cortical steroids are carried bound to plasma proteins, with a free fraction available to act on tissues. Cortisol binds strongly to corticosteroid-binding globulin. Aldosterone also binds proteins but has a larger free fraction.

notes.A: Cholesterol is the precursor of adrenal steroids. It is not itself one of the main adrenal cortical hormones.
notes.C: Catecholamines are released by adrenal medullary chromaffin cells, rather than by the cortex.
notes.D: Steroid metabolites are often conjugated in the liver and excreted chiefly in urine. Biliary excretion is not the predominant route for most of them.
notes.E: Progesterone from the corpus luteum and later the placenta supports pregnancy. This does not describe the adrenal cortical steroids as a class.

questions.stem: Inhibition of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) decreases the:
questions.why: ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Inhibiting ACE decreases this formation pathway and generally reduces angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction and the stimulus for aldosterone secretion.

notes.B: Reduced angiotensin II removes some negative feedback on renin, so renin often rises during ACE inhibition.
notes.C: Urinary flow depends on volume, perfusion and tubular handling. A fall in diuresis is not the primary pharmacological effect.
notes.D: Lower conversion of angiotensin I and increased renin can raise angiotensin I rather than lower it.
notes.E: Lower aldosterone can reduce renal potassium excretion and permit potassium retention.

questions.stem: An adrenal medullary tumour (phaeochromocytoma) may cause an increase in:

options.label: A
options.text: systolic blood pressure which may be transient or constant

questions.why: A phaeochromocytoma can release excess catecholamines, causing sustained or episodic hypertension, tremor and increased energy expenditure. Urinary catecholamines or their metabolites can be elevated. The pattern varies with the tumour and its secretory activity.

notes.A: Adrenergic stimulation can produce persistent or episodic hypertension through vascular and cardiac effects.
notes.B: Excess adrenergic activity can produce a fine tremor, including in the outstretched hands.
notes.C: Catecholamine excess can increase energy expenditure and contribute to weight loss in some people.
notes.D: Tumour catecholamine secretion can increase urinary catecholamines. Metanephrines are generally preferred for biochemical testing.

questions.stem: Excessive glucocorticoid production (Cushing's syndrome) causes an increase in:
questions.why: Chronic glucocorticoid excess increases hepatic glucose output and insulin resistance, leading to higher blood glucose. It can also increase arterial pressure through effects on vascular responsiveness and, in some cases, renal sodium handling.

notes.A: Excess glucocorticoid commonly thins skin through protein catabolism and reduced collagen formation.
notes.B: Bone strength tends to fall because glucocorticoid excess suppresses bone formation and increases fracture risk.
notes.D: Glucocorticoids suppress many inflammatory and immune responses. This can increase susceptibility to infection.
notes.E: Reduced collagen synthesis and impaired inflammatory responses slow wound healing.

questions.stem: Cortisol increases blood glucose level by increasing:
questions.why: Cortisol increases hepatic gluconeogenesis by altering enzyme expression and mobilising substrates. It can also oppose insulin-mediated glucose uptake, helping raise circulating glucose during a sustained stress response.

notes.A: Lipolysis can supply glycerol for gluconeogenesis, but the direct hepatic pathway that produces glucose is gluconeogenesis.
notes.B: Cortisol tends to promote muscle protein breakdown, which provides amino acids that can be used by the liver.
notes.D: Increasing growth hormone release is not the principal mechanism of cortisol-induced glucose production.
notes.E: Insulin normally lowers blood glucose by increasing uptake and restraining hepatic glucose production.

questions.stem: Pancreatic glucagon:

options.label: A
options.text: is produced by the alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans

options.label: C
options.text: output is inversely proportional to the blood glucose level

options.label: D
options.text: increases the breakdown of liver glycogen

questions.why: Glucagon is a peptide from pancreatic alpha cells. Secretion generally rises when glucose falls and decreases after carbohydrate intake, although it is also regulated by other signals. In the liver it promotes glycogen breakdown and glucose production.

notes.A: Pancreatic alpha cells are the principal source of glucagon in the islets of Langerhans.
notes.B: Glucagon is a small peptide hormone, formed by processing the precursor proglucagon.
notes.C: Lower glucose generally stimulates glucagon release, but the relationship is not a fixed inverse proportion across all conditions.
notes.D: Glucagon activates hepatic signalling that increases glycogenolysis and helps maintain circulating glucose during fasting.

questions.stem: Insulin:

options.label: A
options.text: secretion is decreased by sympathetic nerve activity

options.label: B
options.text: facilitates entry of glucose into skeletal muscle

options.label: C
options.text: facilitates entry of amino acids into skeletal muscle

options.label: D
options.text: secretion is increased by vagal nerve activity

questions.why: Insulin promotes uptake of glucose and some amino acids into skeletal muscle and supports protein synthesis. Vagal activity can stimulate meal-related insulin release, while sympathetic alpha-2 signalling usually restrains secretion during stress.

notes.A: Alpha-2 adrenergic signalling on beta cells can decrease insulin release. Other adrenergic receptor subtypes may have different effects.
notes.B: Insulin increases glucose uptake in skeletal muscle by moving GLUT4 transporters to the cell surface.
notes.C: Insulin promotes uptake of some amino acids and supports protein synthesis while reducing proteolysis.
notes.D: Vagal cholinergic activity can stimulate beta-cell secretion and contributes to early meal-related insulin release.

questions.stem: The chemical structure of insulin:

options.label: B
options.text: is identical in all mammalian species

options.label: C
options.text: is such that it is effective when taken by mouth

options.label: D
options.text: has been synthesized in the laboratory

questions.why: Insulin is a peptide with two chains joined by disulphide bonds. Its structure can be reproduced in the laboratory, and human insulin for clinical use can be produced by recombinant DNA methods.

notes.A: Insulin is made of amino acids linked into peptide chains and contains no steroid-type sterol ring.
notes.B: Insulin sequences are similar across many mammals but can differ at particular amino acid positions.
notes.C: Ordinary oral insulin is poorly effective because digestive enzymes can degrade it and intact insulin is poorly absorbed.
notes.E: Laboratory synthesis and recombinant production demonstrate that the insulin molecule can be produced outside the body.

questions.stem: Secretin differs from cholecystokinin-pancreozymin (CCK-PZ) in that it:

options.label: A
options.text: is formed by mucosal cells in the upper small intestine

options.label: B
options.text: stimulates the pancreas to secrete a juice which is rich in digestive enzymes

options.label: C
options.text: stimulates the pancreas to secrete a watery alkaline juice

options.label: D
options.text: has higher effect on gallbladder smooth muscle

questions.why: Secretin is released by duodenal S cells in response to acid and stimulates pancreatic duct cells to secrete watery, bicarbonate-rich fluid. Cholecystokinin mainly stimulates pancreatic acinar enzyme release and gallbladder contraction.

notes.A: Both hormones are made by specialised mucosal cells in the upper small intestine, so their site of origin does not distinguish them.
notes.B: Enzyme-rich secretion is the characteristic cholecystokinin response at the pancreatic acini. Secretin primarily increases ductal bicarbonate.
notes.D: Cholecystokinin is the stronger physiological stimulus for gallbladder smooth muscle contraction after a meal.
notes.E: Secretin participates in intestinal feedback to the stomach and can slow emptying rather than increasing gastric motility.

questions.stem: Insulin:

options.label: A
options.text: requirements at night are similar to those during the day

options.label: B
options.text: half-life is usually reduced in patients with diabetes mellitus

options.label: C
options.text: is mostly bound to plasma proteins in the blood

questions.why: Obesity can increase insulin resistance, so more insulin may be needed to achieve a given metabolic effect. Actual insulin requirements depend on sensitivity, diet, activity and the degree of endogenous insulin secretion.

notes.A: Insulin needs vary over the day with meals, activity and circadian physiology. Day and night doses are not generally assumed equal.
notes.B: Diabetes does not by itself reliably shorten insulin half-life. Clearance depends in part on liver and kidney function and the preparation used.
notes.C: Circulating endogenous insulin is a soluble peptide and is not mostly carried by plasma binding proteins.
notes.E: Exercise can increase muscle glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity, often decreasing rather than increasing insulin needs.

questions.stem: In diabetic ketosis there is a decreased metabolic breakdown of:
questions.why: In diabetic ketosis, insulin deficiency reduces glucose uptake and use in insulin-sensitive tissues even though blood glucose may be high. Increased fatty acid delivery to the liver and beta-oxidation support ketone production.

notes.A: Ketone production exceeds clearance during diabetic ketosis. The core defect is not a general blockade of ketone use.
notes.B: Low insulin and high counter-regulatory signalling can increase breakdown of liver glycogen and hepatic glucose output.
notes.D: Breakdown of adipose triglyceride increases, providing fatty acids for hepatic ketone production.
notes.E: Insulin deficiency can increase proteolysis and the use of amino acids for gluconeogenesis.

questions.stem: An oral glucose tolerance test in a patient with diabetes mellitus shows:

options.label: A
options.text: a higher than normal fasting blood glucose level

options.label: B
options.text: glycosuria when blood glucose is three times the normal fasting level

options.label: C
options.text: a delayed return to the fasting blood glucose level

questions.why: Diabetics have high fasting glucose, renal threshold is exceeded (glycosuria), and glucose remains elevated for a prolonged period after a meal.

notes.A: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.B: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.C: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.E: True, but so are the other statements.
